titulo_longo: Why Japan Erased the Only Survivor of Pearl Harbor's Secret Subs
titulo_short: What Happened to the Only Survivor of Pearl Harbor's Secret Subs?
longo: Ten men went to Pearl Harbor in secret submarines.
Nine of them died. Japan honored them as heroes, and they became known as the Nine War Gods.
The tenth man survived. And Japan struck his name from its records.
This is Kazuo Sakamaki. Brother Quill here. Let's open the book.
When people picture December seventh, 1941, they picture the planes.
But the attack had a second half that almost no one talks about.
Hours before the first bomb, five small submarines were already waiting off Oahu.
Each one had been carried across the Pacific on the deck of a larger submarine.
Their job was to slip into the harbor, wait for the air attack, and fire on the American ships.
They would go in submerged, circle Ford Island, and leave the way they came.
And anything that tried to run, they were to sink as well.
In 1941, a young ensign named Kazuo Sakamaki was brought into that secret program, at the naval base of Kure.
HA-19, the boat he would command, had been built right there at Kure.
The submarine was seventy-eight feet long, with room for two men and two torpedoes.
It ran on batteries, and it was barely six feet wide.
Its top speed was nineteen knots. It also carried a charge of about three hundred pounds, so the crew could destroy it rather than let anyone capture it.
And the crews carried swords and pistols.
According to his memoir, the crews were picked for physical strength and determination.
Twenty-four men were selected. Ten would go on the mission.
They were unmarried men from large families. The logic was cold. The family would survive the loss.
And he wrote that none of them had volunteered. They were told to feel honored.
They trained at Mitsukue Bay, in southern Japan, because its shape resembled Pearl Harbor.
A rendezvous was planned for after the attack, off the island of Lanai. On paper, at least.
But according to his memoir, the batteries would not last long enough to get them back.
Sakamaki did the math. He knew what kind of trip this was.
On November eighteenth, he wrote to his parents.
I owe you, my parents, a debt I shall never be able to repay.

longo.cit: I owe you, my parents, a debt I shall never be able to repay.

longo: The day before the attack, he made a will, and left a lock of hair and his nail clippings for the family altar.
According to his memoir, he dressed for the mission with care: a loincloth, a leather jacket, a headband, and a touch of cherry blossom perfume.
For weeks, the I-twenty-four crossed the Pacific, with the little submarine strapped to its deck.
Then, hours before launch, the final check.
His gyrocompass, the one thing that told him where he was going under water, was broken.
He and his crewman, Kiyoshi Inagaki, tried to fix it. They could not.
By his own account, he was asked if he wanted to back out.
So he went to attack the most important American naval base in the Pacific, nearly blind.
In the early hours of December seventh, the little submarine was released into the dark, about ten miles from the harbor.
Things went downhill, which for a submarine is normally the idea.
With no working compass, he could not hold a course.
Even when they found it, around seven in the morning, they could not get in.
They hit a reef, again and again.
By then, the air attack had begun. The thing he had been sent to join was happening without him.
The destroyer U.S.S. Helm opened fire.
Depth charges shook the hull. Gas from the batteries began to fill it.
According to his memoir, the heat inside reached a hundred and thirty-five degrees.
His torpedoes could no longer fire.
He had crossed the Pacific, and he had not fired a single shot.
He wrote that he wept at the thought of failure.
According to his memoir, he made a new plan: ram an American ship, and die fighting.
The submarine would not even do that. The steering and the power gave out.
It drifted away from the battle, along the coast of Oahu.
Overnight, it ran aground off Bellows Field, on the other side of the island.
American troops guarding the beach could see it on the reef.
He lit the fuse to destroy the submarine, so that it would not fall into American hands.
Then the two men went into the water.
On December eighth, two men of the Hawaii National Guard, Lieutenant Paul Plybon and Corporal David Akui, found Sakamaki in the surf.

lt: Lt. Paul Plybon, Cpl. David Akui

longo: He had commanded a secret weapon. Now he was Prisoner Number One, America's first Japanese prisoner of the war.
He was taken to Fort Shafter, and then to a detention camp on Sand Island.
He asked to be allowed to die. The Americans said no.
One account says he asked again and again. By the same account, his treatment was not harsh.
He told American intelligence officers, my honor as a soldier has fallen to the ground.

longo.cit: My honor as a soldier has fallen to the ground.
longo.sub: Kazuo Sakamaki, to U.S. intelligence officers

longo: Under the code he served, a captured man became a non-person.
For a man raised on that code, there was no way back.
And the Americans had more than the man. They hauled his submarine ashore.
Inside it, they found a chart of his route, drawn right around Ford Island.
None of the five submarines came back.
One was sunk outside the harbor. One got in, fired, missed, and was rammed. Two simply disappeared.
Years later, in 1960, one of those submarines was raised and returned to Japan, where it is on display.
Not his. His was still in America.
Back in Japan, the mission became a legend.
By one account, propaganda even credited a midget submarine with sinking the U.S.S. Arizona. It was destroyed from the air.
Paintings and postcards romanticized the crews.
In March of 1942, the nine dead were promoted two ranks.
In the official painting, there are nine faces.
There was one problem. There had been ten men.
For an officer of Imperial Japan, being captured was considered worse than death.
So they solved it with paperwork. Japan struck his name from its records.
He was not dead. He was simply no longer on the list.
On paper, Kazuo Sakamaki had stopped existing.
Meanwhile, the Americans had found a use for his submarine.
They shipped it to the mainland, studied it, and put it on a truck.
Want to see the enemy's secret weapon? Buy a war bond.
The enemy's secret weapon, it turned out, could be visited for the price of a bond.
On September twenty-fourth, 1942, at Mare Island, California, it was seen by President Roosevelt.
By the end of the war, it was on show in Key West, Florida.
In 1943, it rolled through a small town in Texas called Fredericksburg, the hometown of Admiral Nimitz. Remember that town.
So while Sakamaki sat in a prison camp, his submarine was on tour.
It had a better war than he did.
There is no sign he knew.
And then, in camps across Wisconsin, Tennessee, Louisiana and Texas, something changed.
According to his memoir, he was generally satisfied with how he was treated.
Around the spring of 1942, he began to feel human again, and to see the Americans around him as human too.
His memoir describes something called Internment University.
There were lectures on English, geography, commerce, agriculture, music, Japanese poetry and Buddhist scriptures.
It was a strange sort of college. The students were enemy prisoners, and they had nothing but time.
As new Japanese prisoners arrived, he became a leader among them. He urged them to learn English.
Some arrived ashamed, and wanting to die. They met a man who had once asked for the same thing.
He tried to talk them out of it.
The man Japan had thrown away was now trying to keep its soldiers alive.
He had left as an officer of an empire. He came back to a defeated country, as the man who had not died.
According to his memoir, some of the letters that came were full of hate. One said, I cannot understand how you could return alive.

longo.cit: I cannot understand how you could return alive.

longo: Others came from single women who had heard he was famous. Japan had erased him, but apparently not everywhere.
Then, he wrote, he saw a woman working in a neighbor's field, and fell in love on the spot.
Being careful, he then checked her paperwork. Her health certificate. Her school records. Her family background.
Her name was Sadako. Her father and her brother had died in the atomic bombing of Hiroshima.
She and her mother had moved back to their family home, right next to his.
They married, he wrote, and a daughter followed.
He described them as thin, like so many hard-working Japanese. But, he wrote, above all, we are very happy.

longo.cit: Above all, we are very happy.
longo.sub: Kazuo Sakamaki, I Attacked Pearl Harbor

longo: In 1949, his memoir came out in America, as I Attacked Pearl Harbor.
It had first appeared in Japan, under a plainer title: Four Years as Prisoner of War Number One.
In it, he listed the stages of what he went through: attack, capture, despair, self-contempt, meditation, and finally a wish to help rebuild Japan.

longo.cit: Attack. Capture. Despair. Self-contempt. Meditation. A wish to help rebuild Japan.
longo.sub: The stages he listed in his memoir

longo: After that, he did not speak or write publicly about the war.
He joined Toyota, and worked in exports.
He ended up as production chief of its export division, in Nagoya.
In 1969, he became president of its subsidiary in Brazil.
The man struck from the records was now running a car company on another continent.
In 1983, he went back to Japan.
Back in 1966, the town of Seto, on Mitsukue Bay, had put up a monument to the mission. He was working at Toyota at the time.
He retired in 1987. For decades, not a word.
Then, in 1991, an old man came to Fredericksburg, Texas, for a conference on the Pacific War.
That same town. The hometown of Admiral Nimitz.
The submarine had come to the museum there. It is still there today.
It sits in a display built to look like the deck of the I-twenty-four, on the morning of the attack.
Fifty years after he had left it on a reef, he stood in front of it again.
He was the only man alive who had been aboard that day.
He was reportedly moved to tears.
Kazuo Sakamaki died in 1999, at the age of 81, after a marriage, a career, and a long life he had once asked to give up.
He came to Pearl Harbor to attack America. He spent the next four years learning to see Americans as people, and trying to keep other men alive.
In Japan, on Mitsukue Bay, there is a monument to the men of that mission.
The inscription calls the bay Japan's Pearl Harbor of its time, and now, a Pearl Harbor of peace. The plaque has photographs of nine men.
Behind its plaque stand nine posts, one for each spirit.
short: Ten men went to Pearl Harbor in secret submarines. Nine died, and Japan honored them as heroes. So what happened to number ten?
Kazuo Sakamaki's compass was broken before he launched. He went anyway.
He hit a reef, again and again. A destroyer opened fire. Gas filled the hull, and he lost consciousness. His torpedoes never fired.
He ran aground in Hawaii, and lit the fuse to destroy his sub. It did not explode. His crewman drowned.
He became America's first Japanese prisoner of the war. He asked to be allowed to die. The answer was no.
So Japan struck his name from its records. The official painting shows nine faces.
America put his submarine on a truck, and toured it through forty-one states to sell war bonds.
And according to his memoir, the man who asked to die tried to talk other prisoners out of it.
He came home, joined Toyota, and stayed silent for decades.
Fifty years later, he stood in front of that submarine in Texas, reportedly in tears.
Japan's monument to that mission? It says nine.
